Vignette:
Dr. Thompson still remembers the day the hospital was bombed like it was yesterday. He had just finished a long shift in the emergency room when the sound of shattering glass and screams filled the air. The blast sent him flying across the room, and he landed hard on the floor, disoriented and covered in debris. As he struggled to get to his feet, he saw the chaos around him - patients bleeding, medical staff rushing to respond, and the eerie smell of smoke hanging in the air. In the days that followed, Dr. Thompson was hailed as a hero for his bravery during the attack. But behind closed doors, he began to unravel. He found himself irrationally angry with his wife, snapping at her over minor things, like the way she cooked dinner or the noise level of the TV. His colleagues noticed the change in him too - he became withdrawn and isolated, avoiding discussions about the bombing or anything related to it. As time went on, Dr. Thompson started to feel a creeping sense of unease whenever he rode the bus to work. The sound of screeching tires or the jolt of sudden stops made his heart racing, transporting him back to that fateful day in the hospital. He began to take taxis instead, but even that didn't alleviate the fear. His mind kept wandering to worst-case scenarios - a bomb hidden on board, an attacker lurking among the passengers. One evening, as he was walking home from work, Dr. Thompson caught himself lingering outside his front door, listening intently for any unusual sounds inside. He felt ridiculous, but the habit persisted - every night, without fail. His wife started to notice it too and would sometimes catch him frozen in place, ear pressed against the doorframe. Dr. Thompson couldn't shake off the feeling that people were not what they seemed. Patients who came into his office with seemingly innocuous complaints made him suspicious; he found himself probing for hidden motives or ulterior agendas. His usual warm bedside manner gave way to a detached wariness. The world, in Dr. Thompson's eyes, had become a treacherous place. The thought of another terrorist attack kept him up at night, his mind racing with hypothetical scenarios and countermeasures. He became convinced that he needed to be constantly on guard - that if he let his attention slip for even a moment, disaster would strike. It was this perpetual state of hypervigilance that finally pushed Dr. Thompson's wife to confront him about seeking help. She pointed out how withdrawn he'd become, how the tension between them had grown thick enough to cut with a knife. As they sat in their living room, surrounded by familiar comforts and memories, Dr. Thompson broke down - confessing his deep-seated fears, the suffocating grip of anxiety that had taken over his life. For the first time in years, he let himself admit what he'd been too proud to acknowledge: that the bombing had destroyed a part of him, leaving behind a chasm of distrust and unease. And as the tears streamed down his face, Dr. Thompson realized that it was this very admission - this glimmer of recognition - that made him hope for something more than just getting by; he wanted to rebuild, to rediscover a sense of purpose beyond the trauma's dark shadow. Dr. Thompson now sits in the therapist's office, unsure what lies ahead but ready to confront the demons he's kept at bay for far too long.
